en: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-guhyasamayatantra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of Great Xingshan Temple. The Mahāvairocana,
the All-Illuminating Bhagavat, dwells in the palace of the Dharma-realm, together with the ocean-like assembly of the realm of quiescent light.

Together, experiencing the bliss of the Dharma for themselves, they descend from the Vajra Life-Span of the Tathāgata into the Matrix of Great Compassion (*Mahākaruṇā-garbha*) and speak these verses of self-realization:
"I take refuge in the Dharmakāya of the originally awakened mind, The eternally abiding, wondrous Dharma-lotus throne."
Primordially endowed with the virtues of the three bodies, The thirty-seven honored ones dwell within the city of the mind;
The samādhis as numerous as the atoms of the universal gate, Far removed from cause and effect, naturally possess an ocean of boundless virtues, primordially perfect.
I bow my head and pay homage to all the Buddhas within my own mind.
Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "How are the eight phrases of self-realization to be expounded?

The Bhagavān Mahāvairocana replied to Vajrasattva: "The first four phrases refer to the thirty-seven deities of the Vajradhātu assembly abiding within the lunar disc and moving upon the central terrace.
The latter four phrases refer to the various deities of the eight petals [of the lotus]..."
The Samādhi of the Gate: The Mandala Assembly of Naturalness. The Great Mandala of the Innate Identity and Self-Nature of the Five Courtyards and Two Realms.
Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha once more: "Within the single mind, how is the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma established?"

Regarding the two mandalas, the World-Honored One Vairocana addressed Vajrasattva, saying: "Within the single mind, the wondrous Dharma-lotus constitutes the central terrace of the Vajradhātu Assembly with its thirty-seven wisdoms;
the eight petals are the Universal Gate of the Garbhadhātu Assembly."
[He was] obscured.
Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "I pray that you will expound upon the central platform of the eight petals of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma.
At that time, the Bhagavān Mahāvairocana said to Vajrasattva: "Listen attentively and reflect upon it well. As...
The "Preface Chapter" of the *Secret Lotus Sūtra of the Original Ground* encompasses all the deities of the eight-petaled central platform;
the intermediate chapters reveal the eight petals; and the "Chapter on Encouraging the Aspiration" concludes by returning to the eight petals.

Within these, the twenty-six chapters concern the deities of the eight-petaled central platform through skillful means and parables, while the two chapters concerning the East [concern] the Eastern [deities].

One leaf for Śākyamuni Buddha: the three chapters on the Simile of the Medicinal Herbs and the Bestowal of Prophecy (*Śraddhā-bhaiṣajya-guḍuka-vyākaraṇa*). One leaf for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva in the southeast:

the chapter on the Parable of the City of Illusion (*Gandharva-nagara-upama*). One leaf for Ratnasambhava Buddha in the south: the three chapters on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples and the Dharma Master (*Pañcaśata-pudgala-dharmabhāṇaka-vyākaraṇa*).

One leaf for Mañjuśrī in the southwest. From the Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa to the Chapter on Supernatural Powers (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta* through *Pratihārya-parivarta*), eleven chapters of wondrous [teachings].

This is the internal realization within the central terrace of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, the two Buddhas dwell in the *Jigō* (Nirvāṇa Light) realm; within the Many-Treasures Stūpa, they traverse the assembly in the void.
They entrust [the teaching] to Yakṣa-rāja as the "single leaf" of the Western Quarter. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* entrusts it to Amitābha, the Lord of the Lotus Family.
The two chapters on Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara are likewise the "single leaf" of the Northwest Quarter. The *Dhāraṇī* Chapter belongs to the North.

The single leaf of Fangtiangu Leiyin Buddha; the single leaf of Maitreya Bodhisattva to the northeast of King Wondrous Adornment—likewise, every chapter, every phrase, and every sentence possesses eight petals.
The two chapters that emerge from the Prologue collectively unfold the eight petals of the various honored ones.
The "Expedient Means" and "Life Span" chapters manifest the eight petals, while the "Peaceful Bliss" and "Exhortation" chapters together form the eight petals.
Furthermore, through skillful means, only a Buddha and a Buddha can personally realize the central terrace within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had addressed Śāriputra, Śāriputra took charge of the southeast direction from the eastern gate; this was illustrated by the analogy of the south.

The *Śraddhā-bhaiṣajya* and *Vyākaraṇa* chapters are in the southwest; the *Gandharva-nagara* chapter is in the west; the three chapters on the prophecy for the five hundred people and the Dharma-master are in the northwest;
the *Stūpa* and *Devatā* chapters are in the north; the fourteen preceding chapters from the *Saṃcodana* to the *Maitreya* chapter are the eight petals for the various honored ones;
the *Tathāgata-āyuṣ-pramāṇa* chapter is the central terrace; and the *Vairocana-vibhaṅga* and *Anumodanā* chapters are the eastern gate on one petal.

The "Not Disparaging" chapter is in the west; the "Supernatural Powers" chapter is entrusted to the south; the "Medicine King" chapter is in the northwest; the "Wonderful Sound" and "Avalokiteśvara" chapters are in the northwestern leaf;
the "Dhāraṇī" chapter is in the northern leaf; and the "King Śubhavyūha" chapter is in the northeast.
Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, are Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra the principal deities?
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata replied to Sattva, "Regarding your question: in the first fourteen chapters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Mañjuśrī is the principal deity;
in the latter fourteen chapters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."
He serves as the tutelary deity for them; therefore, in the first fourteen chapters of the Lotus Sutra, Mañjuśrī looks up to him as his guide.
In the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* had Mañjuśrī as its guide;

now, having entered the Dragon Palace, he preaches only the Lotus Sutra to lead the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood in an instant. In the "Chapter on the Peaceful Practices," Mañjuśrī inquires about the peaceful practices.
[The Bodhisattva] proceeded. The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "At the time of the Mañjuśrīdeva-parivarta, what was the appearance of the Honored One as he emerged from the ocean?"
Vairocana spoke thus. At that time, Mañjuśrī sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower, wearing an eight-petaled jeweled crown upon his head;
the great ocean then spontaneously surged forth.
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha again, saying, "Among the eighty thousand great beings, what was the intention for Mañjuśrī alone to enter the dragon palace?
Vairocana replied once more, "Mañjuśrī is the mother of wisdom for all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Within the dragon palace, there are many animals..."
The fool—by means of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom, the folly of the dragon-beast was destroyed. The eight-year-old dragon girl, in a single kṣaṇa, gave rise to the bodhicitta;
in a mere muhūrta, she attained perfect enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha again, saying, "Regarding the fourteen chapters following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, why is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva designated as their presiding deity?
Vairocana replied, "In the 'Exhortation' chapter it says: 'If the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* circulates in Jambudvīpa, there will be those who receive and uphold it.'"
One should form this thought: "All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra.

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, correctly contemplate, understand the meaning and intent, and practice according to the teaching, you should know that such persons are performing the conduct of Samantabhadra."
The *sattva* addressed [Vairocana] again: "Is there a distinction of depth and shallowness regarding the *samayasattva* Samantabhadra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma?
Vairocana spoke again: "Since you yourself are Samantabhadra, why do you ask about yourself? Samantabhadra replied: "There are five levels of difference regarding depth and shallowness."
First is Samantabhadra of Equal Enlightenment; second is Samantabhadra of Wondrous Enlightenment; third is Samantabhadra of Original Enlightenment; fourth is Samantabhadra of Words and Letters;
fifth is Samantabhadra of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the first, the Samantabhadra of Transformation through Equal Enlightenment:

he is the Samantabhadra on the southeast petal of the eight petals of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* [Lotus Sūtra]. Furthermore, he is the Samantabhadra who comes from the east in the "Exhortation" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*).
This is so. Second, the Samantabhadra of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue) is the Ratnasambhava Tathāgata on the southern petal of the eight-petaled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Third, the Samantabhadra of Original Enlightenment (Benjue) is the Mahāvairocana Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment at the central terrace of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The fourth, the Universal Worthy of the Single Syllable, is the Universal Worthy who pervades the Dharma-realm as the non-arising of the single fundamental syllable of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The fifth, the Universal Worthy of True Reality, is the Universal Worthy of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Furthermore, Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "Is there a Svābhāvikakāya Samantabhadra, a Svasaṃbhogakāya Samantabhadra, a Parasambhogakāya Samantabhadra, and a Nirmāṇakāya Samantabhadra?"

Vairocana declared: "First, regarding Samantabhadra as the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body): the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* shows that Samantabhadra relies solely upon suchness (*tathatā*) and not upon a physical realm;
this is Samantabhadra as the Honored One of the self-nature body. Second, regarding Samantabhadra as the *svasaṃbhoga-kāya* (self-enjoyment body):
it is further said that within a single pore of Samantabhadra there are unspeakably many Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust; this is [the self-enjoyment body]."
This is the enjoyment [body] of Samantabhadra. Third, as for the other-enjoyment (parasaṃbhoga) Samantabhadra:

having attained the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) in Akaniṣṭha, he descended to Jambudvīpa below in order to subdue the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist paths and manifested the eight phases of enlightenment;
this is the other-enjoyment Samantabhadra. Fourth, as for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) Samantabhadra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Samant..."
The Bodhisattva Bhaisajyaraja comes from the eastern direction. The *Samantabhadra Sūtra* states that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is born in the Pure and Sublime Land of the East.
The characteristics of that land have already been explained in detail within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. This is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Honored One Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana spoke thus: "There are nine levels of Samantabhadra: first, the Samantabhadra of natural outflow;
second, the Samantabhadra of Equal Enlightenment of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma; third, the Samantabhadra of Wondrous Enlightenment of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma;

fourth, the Samantabhadra of the Original Enlightenment of the Great Sun at the Central Terrace of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma; fifth, the Samantabhadra of the Level [of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma]..."
1. Samantabhadra of the Original Enlightenment of Vairocana Tathāgata; 2. Samantabhadra of the Original Enlightenment of All Dharmas of Vairocana Tathāgata;
3. Samantabhadra of the Single Wheel of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma; 4.
Samantabhadra of the Foremost [Vehicle] of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma; 5. Samantabhadra of the Summit of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma.
At that time, the Sattva wore a crown of the five wisdom-jewels upon his head; his left hand held a vajra-bell, and his right hand held a five-pronged vajra, which he pressed against his heart.
Seated upon a lotus pedestal, he emitted light that illuminated the entire Dharma-realm. He addressed the Bhagavat:
"Now, according to the Buddha’s command, there are three principal deities (bhaṭṭāraka) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: the first is Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Great..."
First, the transformation image of the Tathāgata of the Sun; second, Mañjuśrī as the primary deity (iṣṭadevatā) for the preceding fourteen chapters;
third, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as the primary deity for the subsequent fourteen chapters.

Through the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one enters together into the single palace of original enlightenment, the eternally abiding, primordial ground of immeasurable life, the definitive Tathāgata.
"Hail, Vairocana Tathāgata!
At that time, the Mahāvairocana Tathāgata addressed Vajrasattva, saying: 'Excellent, excellent!'"
One enters deeply into the ocean of the nature of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As you have said, Śākyamuni Mahāvairocana is its primary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*);
likewise, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra Bodhisattvas are also its primary deities.

The ten suchnesses, the true mark, the eight petals, the nine honored ones, and the ten honored ones—these are taught as the virtues of the initial practice of this single division. The nine honored ones of the *Saddharma* are the Lotus [Family].

The seat: the eight petals of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* with the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) at the four corners; the eight petals of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* with the Buddhas of Wondrous Enlightenment (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*) at the four directions.
Within the central terrace of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, the Original Enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*), which is neither cause nor fruit and transcends cause and effect.
Above the Vajra of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment within the Womb Realm (*garbhadhātu*) is the Dharma of Original Enlightenment.
The ocean assembly of the tranquil light of the realms is without beginning or end, its nature and characteristics eternally abiding.

All sentient beings possess within them the eight petals and central platform of the Wondrous Dharma Lotus, along with the ten suchnesses and the ten honored ones; this is called the King of Sutras, the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma.
The Chapter on the Samaya of the Secret Expedient Means of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana addressed Vajrasattva, saying: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
That is to say, all phenomena have such characteristics, such natures, such essences, and such powers."
Thus it is made, thus it has its cause, thus it has its condition, thus it has its fruit, thus it has its retribution; thus, from beginning to end, it is ultimately equal.
This is the first characteristic: the eastern direction, Akṣobhya.
The second, the leaf of nature, is Ratnasambhava in the south;
the third, the leaf of essence, is Amitābha in the west;
the fourth, the leaf of power, is Amoghasiddhi in the north.
Fifth, the *karma-patra* (leaf of action) in the southeast is Samantabhadra;
sixth, the *hetu-patra* (leaf of cause) in the southwest is Mañjuśrī;
seventh, the *pratyaya-patra* (leaf of condition) in the northwest is Avalokiteśvara.
The eighth, the Fruit-Leaf, is Maitreya in the northeast;
the ninth, the Retribution-Leaf, is the Great Japanese Awakened Tathāgata at the center of the platform;
the tenth, the Equal Original Awakening of Beginning and End, is Vairocana Tathāgata.

The eleventh layer consists of the hundred petals, thousand petals, and even unspeakably many petals of the Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment (Honkaku) who is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

These are all the unfolding and transformation of the eight petals of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*). The eight petals of the lotus, the eight seals (*mudrā*), and the central terrace constitute the retribution [body].
Thus, from the beginning to the end, they are ultimately equal; the great wisdom of this equality is the eight petals and the central terrace.
The nine honored ones of equal great wisdom each possess eight petals, eight seals, eight Buddhas, and eight usnīṣas.
On the lowest level are the eight petals; in the middle are the eight seals; and at the summit are the eight Buddhas and eight usnīṣas.
Wherever the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas travel, they manifest vast realms of both defilement and purity, all of which reside upon wondrous Dharma lotuses with eight petals.
The eight petals upon which it rests and the worlds of the eight directions are all that which rests [upon them]. The Buddha-land of Fragrant Accumulation rests upon the central terrace.
The worlds of the ten directions all abide within one mind. One mind has eight petals; because the mind is inexhaustible, the eight petals are inexhaustible.
If the Tathāgata manifests in immeasurable Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, he performs the work of a Buddha by extending his eastern petal;
it is likewise for the other directions and their respective petals.

At that time, Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "World-Honored Buddhas, I pray that you will expound for the great assembly the secret of the four Buddhas' knowledge and vision—the great matter of the appearance of the Buddhas in the world."
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, for the sake of the great assembly, expounded the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma of the Knowledge and Vision of the Four Buddhas;
from the center of its eight petals and the four directions, he revealed the self-realized knowledge and vision of the Four Buddhas, and immediately proclaimed the Heart Mantra to instruct them.
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ ā ā aṃ aḥ sarvabuddha-kīlaya asuravijaya gaganaspharaṇi sarvadharma-buddharīka sattvānugraha hūṃ haḥ vajra-likha maṃ hūṃ svāhā ||
The following was spoken by Vajrasattva himself.
*Namo samantabuddhānām* means "homage to all Buddhas.
*Oṃ* consists of three syllables that contain the single syllable [of the essence]; its function is to provide protection. This is as follows:
The meaning of the perfection of the three bodies (*trikāya*): *A* signifies the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; *A* signifies the revealing of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
*Am* signifies the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; *Aḥ* signifies the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
These are the seed-syllables of the four Buddhas of the four directions. *Sarvabuddha* signifies all Buddhas.
*Jñāna* means "knowledge of meaning. *Sākṣī-vya* means "the vision of meaning," which is the knowledge and vision of the dharma-dhātu.
*Gaganasvabhāva* means "having the nature of space.
*Kṣayi* means "free from suffering. These are all the qualities of skillful means. *Sari*...
The meaning of "Myō" (Miao) is "wondrous. The meaning of "Darma" (Damo) is "Dharma. The meaning of "Fuda yukka" (Fotuoyuejia) is "the eight petals of the white lotus.
The meaning of "Sattaran" (Sadalan) is "sūtra. This, then, is the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma).
*Jaḥ* means "entering. *Hūṃ* means "pervading. *Bam* means "unobtainable. *Hoḥ* means "joy.
*Vajra* means "solid adamant. *Rakṣa maṃ hūṃ* means "emptiness and signlessness.
This is the secret explanation of the remote fundamental meaning; therefore, it is [found in] the *Upāya-paṭala*.
It is said: "To follow" refers to the very meaning of those who have, for kalpas long ago, praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the meaning of emptiness and signlessness: it is because Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva embodies the merit of the three gates of liberation.
Thus, taking Mañjuśrī as the primary deity (honored one), this is the essential heart-mantra of the "Expedient Means" chapter, which is both the provisional means and the ultimate reality.
The Chapter on the Secret Samaya of Seeing the Jewel Stūpa through the Samādhi of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, there was a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels, five hundred yojanas in height, before the Buddha.
Vajrasattva addressed the Bhagavat, saying: "What Buddha is within this jewel stūpa?"
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata addressed the sattva, saying: "Within this precious stūpa is the Great Awakened Lion Throne.
Upon the throne is a precious lotus flower. To the left of the lotus flower is a syllable; the syllable transforms into a great almsbowl. The almsbowl transforms into Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata transforms into Mahāvairocana Tathāgata of the Womb Realm (Garbhakośadhātu). Mahāvairocana...
The Seal of the Dharma-Realm Boundary (Dharmadhātu-vyūha-mudrā) is brought forth. To its right, the seed-syllable transforms into a jeweled stupa (*ratnastūpa*).
The jeweled stupa transforms into the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna transforms into the Vajradhātu Wisdom Fist Seal (*vajrabandha-mudrā*).
The two Buddhas, Mahāvairocana and Garbha-vajra, both enter the ocean of the life-span of a single Buddha without distinction; this is the Decree of Immeasurable Life.
The Tathāgata enters samādhi. Within the moon-disc of his mind is a syllable, which transforms into an eight-petaled lotus.
This eight-petaled lotus pervades the realms of the entire dharmadhātu, benefiting all infinite sentient beings.
The Sattva addressed the Buddha: "I pray that you will explain for me the profound meaning of each individual syllable of the root text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata replied to the Sattva: "Regarding every word and phrase from beginning to end throughout this entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*..."
Every phrase and every syllable is entirely non-syllabic. Syllables are, from the beginning, the true mark (*dharmatā*), fundamentally unarisen.
There are four [aspects] of syllables: first, equality; second, the original vow; third, the removal of hindrances; and fourth, awakening.
The characters are also fourfold: first, pacification; second, augmentation; third, subjugation; and fourth, summoning.

These four are set forth in the introduction, manifested in the main body, and further expanded upon in the dissemination. The six auspicious signs and the characters are the equal and true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, they are equally golden. By receiving this impartial light, one awakens to the equal and true reality.

The *xiāngjìguāng* (Light of Quiescent Characteristics) [chapter] states: "The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, subsequently taught four [teachings] to cause [beings] to awaken to equality.

In the 'Expedient Means' chapter, equality is taught as the primary subject, while the other three are taught incidentally. In the 'Parable of the Burning House,' the original vow is taught as the primary subject, while the other three are taught incidentally.

In the 'Parable of the Poor Son,' the removal of obstacles is taught as the primary subject, while the other three are shown incidentally. In the 'Parable of the Clouds and Rain,' the five hundred [disciples] are taught as the primary subject for the purpose of startling and awakening them, while the others..."

The remaining three [teachings] were proclaimed; the person who recorded them is included herein. Before the Dharma Master circulated [the teachings], the fourfold bodies of the Buddha gathered like clouds to open a single stūpa.
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna served as witness for the fourth. Mañjuśrī constantly transmitted the four gates of rapid [attainment].
The Dragon Girl attained the Way in the South Sea. She made a vow as a *sattva* to sacrifice her body and widely proclaim [the Dharma].
The four dharmas of the syllables; the four modes of peaceful conduct; the practice perfected in a single instant; the emergence of the great assembly from a thousand worlds;
the desire to manifest the Great Maṇḍala of the Original Ground, which is the self that is primordially unborn;

namely, the eternally abiding lifespan of the Tathāgata who has long been accomplished, the essence of the primordially unborn ground of the heart of Mahāvairocana; and even Samantabhadra, who has come from afar since the beginning, makes a renewed request.
The four dharmas are all originally unarisen; it is only by awakening to the fact that my own mind is fundamentally unarisen within the Dharmadhātu—

that the Great Sun Mañjuśrī and the ground of the mind are the syllable of non-arising— that one realizes this is the self-nature of the sentient being's mind, primordially pure, the essence of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma.
The Chapter on the Secret Samaya of Devadatta from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
At that time, Vajrasattva addressed the Bhagavān: "What is the original source of Devadatta?"
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata addressed the Sattva, saying: "Devadatta, Mañjuśrī, and the eight great youths—these are the inconceivable youths of Mount Qingliang.
Therefore, at the time of the Devapada Chapter, the inconceivable youth Mañjuśrī, wearing a jeweled crown of eight-petaled lotuses upon his head, emerged from the ocean and led forth the Naga girls."
Attaining Buddhahood in this very body (*sokushin jōbutsu*). Datta Mañjuśrī; Mañjuśrī’s sword; the Dragon Girl swallowing Mañjuśrī’s sword;
Kūlika; Acala; the fierce and wrathful Acala; Sāgara Dragon King; the appearance of the Seven Buddhas in the world;

the Dragon Girl emerging from the sea and attaining Buddhahood in this very body; mastery over the upper realms of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, and the attainment of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
[The] Jewel. Within the central terrace of the eight-petaled [mandala] of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the immovable central terrace swiftly accomplishes the Way through majestic wrath.

Vajrasattva addressed the Buddha again: "When the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara attains Buddhahood in this very body, may all sentient beings—down to their three souls and seven spirits—and even grasses and trees, attain Buddhahood in this very body. [This is] the Secret [Teaching].
The Prayer of Benediction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the secret mantra for attaining Buddhahood in this very body, saying:
"When this mantra is spoken, grasses, trees, and the entire land shall all equally attain Buddhahood in this very body. *Sālidā*."
Within the initial *kalala* stage of the *māphendalī* flower, there is a ten-colored thousand-petaled lotus.
Within this lotus are one thousand three hundred and ninety-five honored ones. This Buddha suddenly establishes his physical form;
the thousand-petaled white lotus becomes three hundred and sixty white bones, which cover and complete the great, most victorious triple-soul (*trātmaka*).
Within the lunar disc, the Buddha-nature is fully realized; through the samādhi of the wisdom of realization, one attains great sovereign mastery. Furthermore, he spoke this mantra:
"By reciting this mantra, the three souls and seven spirits enter into wondrous enlightenment, and one attains Buddhahood in this very body."
The Chapter on the Secret Samaya of the Tathāgata’s Lifespan in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
At that time, Vajrasattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "O Honored One, Tathāgata of Realization from Time Immemorial, I pray that you will graciously reveal your sublime form."

Mahāvairocana Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva, saying: "The Tathāgata of the True Attainment of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma from Long Ago has been dwelling serenely and eternally within the original Many-Jeweled Stūpa. His name is the Tathāgata Infinite Life Sovereign King of Certainty.
He forms the Dharma-Realm Seal with his hands, and upon his head he wears a jeweled crown featuring two Buddhas. On the left side of the crown is Śākyamuni Tathāgata."
In the Womb Realm (Garbhadhātu), to the right of Vairocana Tathāgata, there is Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata; this is the Vajradhātu.

Vairocana Tathāgata always resides within the stūpa. In the eastern gate of the Jewel Stūpa of the ocean-like assembly of the Cloud-Gathered Manifestations of the Same-Body Essential Nature Vairocana Tathāgata, there is the Bodhisattva Ūrdhvagama; at the southern gate, there is Anantagati.
As for the Bodhisattvas: at the western gate is the Bodhisattva Śuddhacaryā; at the northern gate is the Bodhisattva Sthitacaryā.

These four Bodhisattvas correspond to the four Buddhas of the four directions; therefore, they seal the seals of the four Buddhas. Furthermore, in the southeast of the precious stūpa is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
in the southwest is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī; in the northwest is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; and [in the northeast is] Maitreya.

To the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara: At the central hub of the eight petals of the Lotus of the Sublime Dharma, within the ocean-like assembly of the three families whose essence is identical to Vairocana, during the fifty billion *paramāṇu*-dust eons, the Tathāgata King of Infinite Life and Certainty spoke this heart-mantra:
Namo ārya-maitreyanātha-vinaiśvara-tathāgatāya | Oṃ sarvasaṃskāra-pariśuddha-dharmate mahānaya-parivare svāhā ||
Vajrasattva said: "Namo" is the word for taking refuge;
"Aruṇimite" is the word for the eastern direction; "Ucchiṣṭa" is the word for the southern direction;
"Viṇmūtraśe" is the word for the western direction; and "Rāśidhara" is the word for the northern direction.
The phrase *tathāgata* is the central platform. *Oṃ* is the central platform among the three bodies (*trikāya*);
since the eight petals are all endowed with the three bodies, the syllable *oṃ* is placed in the middle of the mantra.
*Sarvasaṃskāra* is the southern phrase. *Parivartate*.
*Dharmate* is the phrase of Mañjuśrī; *mahānaya* is the phrase of Avalokiteśvara;
*parivāre* is the phrase of Maitreya; and *svāhā* is the phrase of definitive accomplishment. This contains profound secrets.
At that time, Vajrasattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "Where is the Tathāgata Long-Age-Realized (Cirotpannasiddha)?
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata replied to Sattva, "Within the single thought-moment of the mind of all sentient beings, there is the Tathāgata;
his lifespan is so long and his body is such a sea of tranquil light that even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas cannot know it. For this reason, Mi..."
Having pressed me three times, the Tathāgata then proclaimed the four admonitions.
Vajrasattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in what passage of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the ocean of the serene light of a single thought expounded?"

The World-Honored One declared: “The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* proclaims to sentient beings that upon hearing of the Buddha’s long life-span, they may attain faith and understanding in a single thought-moment.
The Tathāgata perceives and knows the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth-and-death;

Vairocana pervades all places, and the dwelling place of that Buddha is eternally the Light of Quiescence (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*). Through the Tathāgata’s prajñā, he perceives and knows the triple world and the six realms of existence.”
Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean are originally empty space, without birth or death; they are the eternally quiescent light of Great Parinirvāṇa.
That sentient beings do not know this is called ignorance, the beginning of birth and death.

The first part of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) says: "By means of the profound *prajñā*, I have universally observed all the mountains, great oceans, the vast earth, and sentient beings within the three realms and the six paths.
Thus, the fundamental nature of these three realms is detached, ultimately quiescent, and identical in character to empty space.
It is without name or consciousness, forever severing all modes of existence (*bhava*). From the beginning, it is equal, without high or low."
Characteristics: they are without seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing; they cannot be bound and cannot be liberated;
they are without sentient beings and without life-span; they are neither born nor arisen, neither exhausted nor extinguished;
they are neither worldly nor non-worldly; and both nirvana and saṃsāra are unattainable. One who knows this is called a world-transcender. Not knowing these matters is called birth.
The beginning of death. You, the great assembly, should sever ignorance and extinguish the beginning of birth and death.

Contemplate universally that all sentient and non-sentient beings, and all persons and phenomena within the three realms, are ultimately nothing other than this: they do not exit the three realms, nor do they enter into any state of existence.
They are primordially pure, stainless, and free from afflictions, equal to empty space. They are neither unequal nor not unequal. Exhausting all...
When movement of thought ceases and the mind of conceptualization subsides, such a dharma-characteristic is called Great Nirvana. He further addressed the great assembly:
"With my Buddha-eye, I have observed all dharmas throughout the triple world. The fundamental limit of ignorance is by nature originally liberated;
one cannot find its source even by searching throughout the ten directions. Because it has no cause, its branches and leaves are all entirely liberated. Ignorance is liberation."
Therefore, they attain liberation from everything up to old age and death. For these reasons, I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence, which is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this is from the "Chapter on the Secret Samaya of the Tathāgata’s Lifespan" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Vajrasattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the presence of the Tathāgata King of Certainty with Immeasurable Life, who has long since truly attained accomplishment, is there the Buddha-dharma?"
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them, saying: "The Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, Perfectly Accomplished from Long Ago, possesses eight stages.

First is the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma of the Original Ground of Equal Enlightenment from Long Ago; its eight petals and four Bodhisattvas represent the Honored Ones of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment.

Second is the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma of the Original Ground of Perfect Enlightenment, Perfectly Accomplished from Long Ago; its eight petals and four Buddhas [represent the Stage of Perfect Enlightenment]."

First, the Honored One of the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Second, the Original Ground (*mūlabhūmi*) of the True Accomplishment of Wondrous Enlightenment, which is the Central Terrace of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Third, the Mahāvairocana Tathāgata of the Central Terrace of the True Accomplishment of the Original Ground, who is the Original Awakening (*mūlajñāna*), and the four Buddhas of the eight petals, who are the Initial Awakening (*ādikarmika-bodhi*) Tathāgatas.
Fourth, above the Original Awakening of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata of the Central Terrace of the Original Ground, there is a wondrous...

The Lotus of the Dharma. Among the Tathāgatas of the Central Terrace of Original Enlightenment and the Tathāgatas of the Eight Petals of the Four Buddhas, those below constitute *shikaku* (initial enlightenment).
The Central Terrace alone is the Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment. This is the ninth, the Great Vairocana of the Reward Terrace of Original Enlightenment;
he descends as the tenth, the Vairocana Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment in which the ultimate equality of beginning and end is realized.

From the fundamental phase of the eight-petaled leaves up to the ultimate retribution of the central platform of Mahāvairocana Tathāgata, all are equal to the fundamental awakening (honkaku) of the Tathāgata;
thus, the stage of the fundamental awakening is supreme. Fifth, above the equality of the fundamental awakening Tathāgata are the fundamental awakening of all dharmas, Vairocana Tathāgata;
even this equality of the fundamental awakening of Vairocana Tathāgata is still [surpassed].

The nine honored ones of the central platform within the eight petals are the nine dharma-bodies of original enlightenment (*honkaku*). All other phenomena, such as the nine dharma-realms (*hokkai*), are likewise original enlightenment;
even the Buddha’s lower manifestations are the original enlightenment of Vairocana Tathāgata. The myriad phenomena of the nine dharma-realms are all the Tathāgata of original enlightenment.
Reaching down to every single atom of dust, they all come to pay homage and look up to [the Buddha] as the Tathāgata of original enlightenment.
Come. Sixth: Among the dharmas of the Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment (Hon-gaku), there is the single wheel-dharma;

because the triple-layered Tathāgata of Original Enlightenment falls into the original enlightenment of initial awakening (Shi-gaku), even the single wheel of the original enlightenment of initial awakening does not stand, for it is a dharma that is fundamentally unarisen and thus resides above original enlightenment. Seventh: The first dharma upon the single wheel is the word "single wheel" (Ichin).
The seed-syllables of the wheel of letters, the seed-syllables, the samaya-forms, and the forms of the Honored Ones possess both signs and signlessness;

while these are expedients for the ignorant, in reality they abide solely in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This ultimate reality is supreme. Eighth, regarding the meaning of this ultimate reality:
because even the meaning of reality conforms to the ultimate meaning, it is the unique crown atop the summit, not within the measure of the ignorant; it is the highest pinnacle of reality.
The Chapter on the Secret Samaya of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging from the Samādhi of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma.
At that time, Vajrasattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "In what manner does the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging pay homage?"
Mahāvairocana Tathāgata declared: "The 'Ever-Venerable' (Sadāparibhūta) means that 'ever' refers to a single prostration, while 'venerable' refers to all prostrations.
It means knowing and seeing the lotus-heart of sentient beings and performing prostrations, rather than specializing solely in the recitation of scriptures.
Merely practicing prostrations and placing faith in the syllable-gateway *praṃ*, one prostrates to Mahāvairocana Tathāgata at the central platform; this is called 'a single prostration. Binding...
The "Gate of Characters" (Akṣaramukha) is the severance of the path of speech. Above it is a single dot, which is the Great Emptiness (Mahāśūnyatā).
The Great Emptiness is the inconceivable; the Dharma of the Self is wondrous and difficult to fathom. One should simply practice prostrations—four prostrations:

first, prostrate to the nature of the Vajra Family; second, prostrate to the nature of the Ratna Family; third, prostrate to the nature of the Dharma Family; fourth, prostrate to the nature of the Karma Family. These are called all prostrations.
I pay homage to the Buddha-nature, which is the eternally abiding mark of the world. I pay homage to the letter-gateway *li*. I pay homage to the letter-gateway *li*.
I pay homage to the nature of the Dharma-body of the intrinsic nature of the Vajra Family. I pay homage to the Buddha-nature in which afflictions are themselves bodhi.

I pay homage to the letter-gateway *tra*. I pay homage to the letter-gateway *tra*. I pay homage to the nature of the Dharma-body of the merit of the Ratna Family. I pay homage to the liberation of karmic bonds as they are.
To liberate the Buddha-nature: I pay homage to the *ghri* syllable-gateway; I pay homage to the *ghri* syllable-gateway. I pay homage to the nature of the wisdom-dharmakāya of the Dharma division.
I pay homage to the Buddha-nature wherein birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa. I pay homage to the *ma* syllable-gateway; I pay homage to the *ma* syllable-gateway.
I pay homage to the nature of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Karma division. I prostrate to all of them; one prostration is every prostration.
Vajrasattva again addressed the Buddha, saying, "Should one not pay homage to grasses, trees, lands, and so forth, as the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati does?
Vairocana Buddha replied, "One should dwell deeply in prostration. As you have asked, the essence-nature of the Dharma-realm is non-discriminative;
the myriad phenomena of the universe are themselves the Dharmakāya. Therefore, I pay homage to all atoms of dust."

In the "Chapter on the Secret Samaya of the Dharani of the Samadhi of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma," Vajrasattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "What is the original source of the ten rakshasas and the others?"
Vairocana Buddha spoke, saying: "The ten rākṣasīs originally possess three types of awakening: first, equal awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); second, wondrous awakening (*vimalā-bodhi*);
and third, original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). The first four rākṣasīs correspond to the four great bodhisattvas of pure conduct; the fifth rākṣasī corresponds to Śākyamuni;
the middle four rākṣasīs correspond to the four great bodhisattvas of the eight petals; and the tenth rākṣasī..."
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, furthermore, has ten rākṣasīs; these ten are such honored forms. Eight rākṣasīs are the eight petals, which are thus.
The ninth is Gaudī, which is thus. The tenth is the rākṣasī whose beginning and end are ultimately equal.
On the third day of the tenth month in the twenty-first year of Ōei (the Jia-wu year), the Head of the Multō Peak Academy personally transcribed this and entrusted it to the elder monk Muzan.
The elder monk, having received these instructions, was admonished again and again, saying: "This is the jewel within the topknot.
Do not let it leak out through negligence; be most diligent in its preservation."
This is the place where the imperial manuscript was transcribed, presented on the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month in the thirty-fourth year of the Eikyō era (Jinwei).
The Venerable Yūkū said: "The scriptures brought back by the Great Master Kōbō Daishi state:"
It remains a secret treasury of the Infinite (Mujaku). Herein, the two scrolls concerning Prince Ryōshu at Tōbō Peak were transcribed as they were seen;
see the notes for details. It is said that the six *Jizō-hongengenshi* (Origins of the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha) are fully detailed therein.
Is this not different from this sutra? One should pursue and investigate it further. This is the secret manuscript transmitted by Ryōsei of the Shōzō-bō.
It is indeed so. It is profoundly secret, profoundly secret; one must not harbor other views (and so forth).
Written by Kongo Saiben (Shōnin Ryōmyō of An’yō-ji, Sakamoto), on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month in the ninth year of Eikyō (the Ding-si year), at the North Valley of Hōdō-in, Sannomine.
In the Hōkō-bō, he no longer heeded the ridicule of those with shallow pens nor the slanders of later observers;
he devoted himself solely to his resolve to seek the Dharma, recording it like the script of bird tracks.
Postscript by Kimgang Chongun (age fifty-one, thirty-eight years since ordination) following the *Sālendrarāja-samādhi-sūtra*:
As for the *Sālendrarāja-samādhi-saddharma*, it was answered by the Tathāgata Vairocana.
It sets forth the Questions of Vajrasattva and reveals the Primordial Secret and Sublime Treasury.

It proclaims the secret mantras for the attainment of Buddhahood in this very body (sokushin jōbutsu) for all sentient and non-sentient beings—including the three souls and seven spirits—as well as for even grasses and trees.
My Great Ancestor Master has inscribed this title upon the *Unobstructed Sūtra of the Great Lotus Family*. Herein it is raised:
The eight-line verse of self-realization within the sūtra establishes the principle of attaining Buddhahood in this very body (*sokushin jōbutsu*).
Regarding what is called the *Padmasamādhi-sūtra*, although its name was known in our country, the sūtra itself had not been seen.

When Great Master Kūkai entered Tang China and visited the Venerable Huiguo, he successfully received the transmission of the Dharma and the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*); however, as for the *Padmasamādhi-sūtra*...

This most profound secret dharma cannot be transmitted [otherwise]. It is transmitted solely by means of the verse beginning with "I take refuge in the Dharmakāya of the mind of original enlightenment" (and so forth, until) "I prostrate to the Buddhas of the mind" (text).

However, according to the *Kanji Kan* (Examination of Characters), the *Kaibushi-ki* (Record of Kaihō) cites the *Lotus Samādhi Sūtra* as its source to authenticate this as his own oral teaching. Viewed from this perspective...
It is certainly not merely that these are not the eight-line *svasaṃvedana-gāthā*. The *Guxiang ji* (Collection on Echoes in Valleys), fascicle ten, states:
"The oral instructions transmitted through the patriarchal lineage of the Tiantai school state: 'The *Lotus Samādhi Sūtra* is also called the *Sūtra of Non-obstruction*.
Its full title is the *Sūtra of the Secret Samaya of the Lotus Samādhi of the Sublime Dharma*. Great Master Chishō extracted ten [passages] from it."
From the middle volume, the essential request states (in the text): "Generally, these secret scriptures consist of two fascicles:
namely, the present secret scripture and the scripture that explains the original ground of the Six Kṣitigarbha Honored Ones.

In the middle ten days of the first summer month of the fourteenth year of the Genroku era, the man from Yue, Ryō, harboring the humble aspiration to transmit the lamp and protect the Dharma, traveled with his staff to the Northern Capital to pay his respects.
The Great Sōjō (Chief Abbot) En of Shinjō-in on the Western Mountain personally transmitted and orally translated [the text], fully fulfilling my aspirations.
I returned to pay homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva at Ninnō-ji and stayed overnight at An’yō-an, where I fortunately found this scripture within the storehouse. My joy was boundless;
how truly rare it is! This is a blessed gathering for a hundred generations and a fortunate encounter for a thousand years. Thereupon, I took up my brush...

I have long been engaged in copying this work; however, upon reading it carefully from time to time, I find that expanded passages, omitted characters, inverted words, and scribal errors are frequent.

Sighing deeply, I could not set down the scroll without feeling sorrowful and lamenting. This year, the Abbot Xunxu of Fengshan West Cloister and the Abbot Chunchuan of Luoshan in Donghai, both of whom possess ancient manuscripts, kindly provided me with their texts.
Thus, having compared these two versions of the scripture, I have once again transcribed it by hand with great care.
I have sought out and disseminated these auxiliary instructions to bequeath them to future generations. Nevertheless, there may still be some lingering doubts;

it is my hope that later scholars will await this work to obtain what is correct and properly refine the fundamental text. May it be edited for purity, brilliantly polished, and circulated so that its benefits flow like water from a spring, nourishing the withered and making the wondrous Dharma—both flower and fruit—thrive and endure long.
Thus, the true wind shall be raised, and the lotus in the heart-ground shall bloom. So it is said.
On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of the year of the Dragon (Xinmao), the first year of the Zhengde era, the bhikṣu Xingliang, who transmits the Yoga teachings,
records his profound thoughts at the Southern Pavilion of Bianzhao Yuan on the rocky cliffs of Lunsan.
